251.t: Beansy's son and a failed attempt to book the band again
251.s: After giving up his band, Albert let Beansy's son finance and book it; the venture failed and Albert rebooked it himself.
251.q: Y-L-E-N-D. Yeah. I'd never seen his name written on him. I didn't know how to spell it on him. Right. Well, he confidants Beansy.

251.t: Business manager, bad bookers and breaking up in 1940
251.s: Cottrell was business manager; a bad booker, Al Travis, wrecked plans, and Albert disbanded in 1940.
251.q: Take care of little incidental and demand, such as bookkeeping, paying off the musicians, calling the rehearsals, and various things like that. And I would have time on the job, intermissions.

387.t: How Sauter-Finegan ended and the State Department tour
387.s: The band disbanded over taxes and losses and was passed over for State Department tours.
387.q: A couple of years; we disbanded--the government was threatening to take all the money at the gate to pay the taxes we owed them, and that would have left us stranded who knows where, and we were constantly being sent out on the road, at a loss. We never made any money with that thing, not enough to…

387.t: How the band ended: tax threat and losses
387.s: Willard Alexander wanted a dance band; the tax at the gate ended it.
387.q: Ever since the first time out, we began losing money and it was suggested from the agency, Willard Alexander agency, that we cut down the size of the band and stop playing what we're doing and play dance music. I'm sure that Miller's getting that too, that's the only thing he knows when it comes…

970.t: Who directed the WPA band, and cutting it down to c. 1938
970.s: Louis Domaine directed the band while another man ran the project and picked out bad notes; the band was cut down around 1938. They talk about framing and keeping the photos.
970.q: Yeah, he had the band in charge, you see. Yeah, he was, Louis Domaine was directing the band. But he was supposed to be the director, but he'd put another man of the band. Sort of in charge of the band. Sort of in charge of the whole project or something. Oh, that's right. Yeah, I didn't know how…

603.t: Building a jazz group with Capitol deal, then collapse
603.s: With Mike Wofford, Richie Matteson and Kay Brown he gets a Capitol deal, but the group walks out at Tahoe leaving him in debt; Frank Ross urges him to go solo.
603.ch: Vegas groups and Spokane solo years
603.q: Yeah. Anyway this guy Lee Dear said, “Look, why don’t you put together the group that you want and I’ll sign the contract, you can stay here.” So I got Mike Wofford on piano, who is an internationally known jazz player, a bass player from Lake Tahoe named Chuck DeLora who is a great player, Richie…

459.s: Leaders paid sidemen from their own pockets, lost $90,000; Sauter went to Baden Baden, Finegan stayed in New York.
459.q: Yeah. Well it got so bad at one point where the leaders took twenty-five dollars apiece for themselves just to be able to pay the guys in the band. And we didn’t want that. So the band folded. We did just weekends. I left the band, I had left the band, a lot of guys had left the band, and the band…

504.t: Compost's gigs, Lee Morgan's death and the Columbia records
504.s: An opening slot for Yes on the night Lee Morgan was shot; without money for touring the band folds after two records.
504.ch: CTI, Compost and the first Directions
504.q: hear this music. He thought we were a typical Rock N’ Roll band. It was little more sophisticated than he expected. Nonetheless, I got quite a nice deal with Columbia to do 4 records. We split the contract five ways instead of it just being me, and I decided I wanted to make it a co-op band. At…

99.t: Chambers books Dizzy Gillespie and the band must lay off
99.s: On their return the Club Riviera owner gives their three weeks to Dizzy Gillespie, and Pillars and Jeter pay the musicians out of pocket.
99.ch: Last years of the band and reflections
99.q: trip ended in New York City. And we had booked our band back in the Club Riviera. We had given Mr. Chambers the first three weeks of fall, in St. Louis. He took advantage of us, and let a booking agent book Dizzy Gillespie in for that three weeks, and that made us have to lay off for three weeks.…

19.t: Eckstine gives up the big band and offers him $100 a week
19.s: With the war over and debts of about $25,000, Eckstine goes solo and asks Malachi to be his pianist and musical director.
19.ch: Trio, Eckstine accompanist and Illinois Jacquet, 1945-48
19.q: It was around late summer of 1947 that Billy Eckstine finally gave up his band, because the War was over and all the principal guys had left. And he had good men in his band. He had acquired tenor saxophonist Frank Wess. By this time Miles Davis was in New York, and he had Miles Davis in the band.…
